name: Unconditional Positive Regard
definition: The practice of completely accepting and supporting another person without judgment, reservations, or contingent evaluation.
mechanism: Removes the threat of social rejection, allowing the individual's defense mechanisms to disarm so their genuine internal conflicts can be explored.
example: A parent listening calmly and lovingly to a teenager confessing to breaking a curfew, without withdrawing affection or berating.

name: Empathy
definition: The ability to accurately perceive and understand the internal emotional state and subjective perspective of another person.
mechanism: Engages mirror neurons and medial prefrontal circuits to construct an emotional simulation while maintaining self-other boundaries.
example: A friend sitting with you after a pet passes away, understanding your grief deeply rather than offering unsolicited silver linings.

name: Active Listening
definition: A disciplined communication technique requiring full attention, cognitive paraphrasing, and non-verbal feedback to verify understanding.
mechanism: Combines auditory working memory with reflective verbal synthesis, signaling psychological safety and validating the speaker's emotional state.
example: A manager summarizing an upset employee's feedback in her own words before replying with possible solutions.

name: Congruence
definition: The state of harmony where an individual's outward expressions and actions match their genuine internal feelings and self-concept.
mechanism: Reduces chronic autonomic nervous stress caused by maintaining false social facades, fostering psychological authenticity.
example: Saying you are disappointed with a project outcome honestly instead of smiling and pretending everything is fine while feeling resentful.

name: Cognitive Restructuring
definition: A therapeutic process of identifying, challenging, and reframing automatic irrational or distorted thought patterns.
mechanism: Uses conscious prefrontal cognitive control to interrogate automatic limbic catastrophic interpretations and establish balanced alternatives.
example: Changing 'I made a typo in my report, so I will be fired' to 'It was a minor mistake that I can easily correct in the next version.'

name: ABC Model
definition: A cognitive framework demonstrating that external Activating events (A) do not directly cause emotional Consequences (C); our Beliefs (B) mediate the reaction.
mechanism: Exposes the internal interpretive filter that converts neutral situational sensory input into emotional distress.
example: Two people receive identical critical email reviews; one feels crushed believing they are worthless, while the other feels motivated to clarify the requirements.

name: Free Association
definition: A psychoanalytic method where a person speaks aloud whatever thoughts, memories, or sensations arise without conscious censorship.
mechanism: Bypasses conscious ego defenses and working-memory filtering to bring unconscious emotional conflicts into verbalized awareness.
example: Saying random words triggered by an inkblot or image until an unexpected childhood memory of moving houses spontaneously emerges.

name: Transference
definition: The unconscious redirection of childhood feelings, expectations, and attitudes toward a new person or therapist in the present.
mechanism: Relies on pre-existing attachment schemas that project historical interpersonal dynamics onto neutral contemporary relationships.
example: Becoming unexpectedly defensive toward a mentor simply because their posture or tone of voice mirrors an overly critical older sibling.

name: Defense Mechanisms
definition: Unconscious psychological strategies used to protect the conscious mind from intolerable anxiety, guilt, or painful realities.
mechanism: Suppresses, redirects, or rationalizes distressing internal or external stimuli to prevent ego distress and autonomic overwhelm.
example: Channeling frustration from an unfair traffic ticket into vigorously cleaning the kitchen or running five kilometers (sublimation).

name: Self-Actualization
definition: The innate psychological drive to realize one's fullest individual capabilities, creative potential, and intrinsic purpose.
mechanism: Emerges when physiological, safety, belonging, and self-esteem needs are sufficiently satisfied, shifting motivation toward growth.
example: An accountant dedicating evenings to composing chamber music purely for creative expression and personal fulfillment.

name: Locus of Control
definition: The degree to which people believe that life outcomes are determined by their own actions (internal) versus external forces (external).
mechanism: Calibrates perceived agency, influencing whether an individual initiates active problem-solving or succumbs to fatalistic inaction.
example: Attributing an exam result to study habits and preparation rather than luck or unfair exam questions.

name: Motivational Interviewing
definition: A collaborative, goal-oriented counseling style designed to strengthen personal motivation and commitment to a specific change by resolving ambivalence.
mechanism: Encourages the client to voice their own arguments for change ('change talk'), shifting cognitive dissonance into self-driven resolution.
example: A coach asking open questions about how better sleep would improve a student's morning alertness rather than lecturing on bedtime rules.

name: Systematic Desensitization
definition: A behavioral therapy technique pairing deep relaxation with gradual, stepped exposure to a feared object or scenario.
mechanism: Utilizes reciprocal inhibition to replace autonomic sympathetic fight-or-flight panic with parasympathetic calmness in the amygdala.
example: Overcoming fear of public speaking by first imagining a friendly audience while breathing deeply, then speaking to one friend, and gradually expanding to a room.

name: Therapeutic Alliance
definition: The cooperative and affective bond between client and practitioner, united by shared goals and mutual trust.
mechanism: Creates a secure attachment container that dampens social threat appraisal and amplifies treatment adherence across modalities.
example: A student feeling safe enough to admit their fear of thesis failure knowing their mentor will listen without judgment.

name: Reframing
definition: Altering the conceptual and emotional viewpoint from which a situation is experienced to uncover productive new meanings.
mechanism: Shifts contextual perceptual framing, engaging alternative associative memory networks to re-evaluate subjective emotional valence.
example: Viewing an unexpected project cancellation not as wasted effort, but as an opportunity to harvest the reusable code for a bigger initiative.

name: Johari Window
definition: A psychological model mapping interpersonal awareness across four quadrants: Open, Blind, Hidden, and Unknown self.
mechanism: Balances self-disclosure and constructive feedback to expand mutual understanding and decrease defensive blind spots.
example: Learning in a team retrospective that teammates find your rapid silence intimidating rather than thoughtful as you had assumed.

name: Genogram
definition: A multi-generational visual family tree diagram detailing psychological dynamics, medical histories, and recurring behavioral patterns.
mechanism: Externalizes complex transgenerational systemic scripts onto a spatial map, facilitating objective pattern recognition.
example: Tracing how career choices or conflict avoidance strategies have subtly repeated across grandparents, parents, and siblings.

name: Attachment Theory
definition: A developmental framework showing that early relational bonds with primary caregivers form enduring internal working models of intimacy and security.
mechanism: Programs autonomic stress reactivity and interpersonal expectation schemas during critical neurodevelopmental periods.
example: A person comfortably asking a romantic partner for reassurance during a stressful week because they trust relationships are secure.

name: Zone of Proximal Development
definition: The developmental sweet spot between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with knowledgeable guidance.
mechanism: Optimizes cognitive load by offloading task complexity to a more experienced mentor while active learning circuits consolidate.
example: A coding mentor showing a student how to debug a pointer error with guiding questions rather than writing the fix for them.

name: Object Permanence
definition: The cognitive understanding developed in infancy that physical objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen or heard.
mechanism: Establishes internal mental representation in the parietal and frontal cortices independent of real-time sensory perception.
example: An infant delightedly searching beneath a blanket for a toy rather than assuming it vanished when covered.

name: Conservation
definition: The cognitive ability to understand that fundamental properties like volume, mass, or quantity remain identical despite changes in outward appearance.
mechanism: Requires decentering and mental reversibility in operational thought, overcoming simple perceptual salience.
example: Understanding that pouring water from a short wide glass into a tall thin beaker does not create more water.

name: Egocentrism
definition: The cognitive inability to distinguish between one's own subjective perspective and someone else's viewpoint.
mechanism: Reflects incomplete maturation of the temporoparietal junction, which is responsible for perspective-taking computations.
example: A young child holding up a picture facing themselves and asking 'Look, do you like this drawing?' without turning it toward you.

name: Psychosocial Stages
definition: An eight-stage lifespan model where personal growth emerges from successfully resolving distinct psychosocial crises at each developmental epoch.
mechanism: Integrates biological maturation with expanding social expectations, forming the scaffolding of identity and ego strength.
example: A college student navigating 'Identity vs Role Confusion' by exploring diverse career paths, values, and research interests.

name: Critical Period
definition: A biologically bounded window of time during which specific environmental stimulation must occur for normal neural development to take place.
mechanism: Driven by heightened synaptic plasticity and BDNF expression, followed by permanent myelination and synaptic pruning.
example: A child acquiring native phonetic fluency and accentless pronunciation in multiple languages before early adolescence.

name: Imprinting
definition: A rapid, phase-sensitive form of learning that occurs during a narrow early developmental window, establishing an instinctive social attachment.
mechanism: Hardwires immediate visual-olfactory cues in the hyperstriatum to guarantee proximity to a protector for survival.
example: Newly hatched ducklings following a human caregiver as if they were their biological mother.

name: Scaffolding
definition: Temporary instructional support tailored to a learner's current competence, gradually withdrawn as independence increases.
mechanism: Prevents executive function overload by structuring sub-goals, keeping the learner within their optimal attentional zone.
example: A driving instructor first handling steering while the student works the pedals, before handing over complete vehicular control.

name: Theory of Mind
definition: The cognitive capability to attribute mental states—beliefs, desires, intentions, and knowledge—to oneself and others, recognizing they may differ.
mechanism: Coordinated recruitment of the medial prefrontal cortex and temporoparietal junction to simulate another person's subjective epistemic state.
example: Understanding that a colleague was late to a meeting because their train broke down, rather than assuming they were intentionally disrespectful.

name: Identity vs Role Confusion
definition: The fifth psychosocial stage where adolescents experiment with roles and values to forge a coherent sense of personal self.
mechanism: Integrates episodic autobiographical memory with social feedback to synthesize a stable core self-schema.
example: A university student trying out student government, theater, and lab research to figure out who they genuinely want to be.

name: Kohlberg's Moral Stages
definition: A six-stage developmental sequence tracing moral reasoning from obedience to avoid punishment up to universal ethical principles.
mechanism: Reflects the cognitive shift from concrete perceptual self-interest toward abstract societal perspective-taking.
example: Returning a lost wallet because honesty is an ethical duty (post-conventional), rather than simply fearing a security camera fine (pre-conventional).

name: Cognitive Map
definition: An internal mental representation of the spatial relationships and layout of one's physical or conceptual environment.
mechanism: Constructed via place cells in the hippocampus and grid cells in the entorhinal cortex computing allocentric spatial vectors.
example: Navigating your hometown's back alleys effortlessly even when a major street is closed for construction.

name: Working Memory
definition: A limited-capacity cognitive system responsible for temporarily holding, updating, and manipulating information during complex reasoning.
mechanism: Coordinated between the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive in the prefrontal cortex.
example: Calculating a 15% tip in your head while continuing a pleasant dinner conversation.

name: Cognitive Offloading
definition: The physical or digital reliance on external tools to reduce the cognitive demands of remembering, calculating, or navigating.
mechanism: Metacognitive monitoring assesses the mental cost of internal retention against tool retrieval cost, choosing the path of least cognitive resistance.
example: Typing a six-digit verification code into a notes app or immediately using GPS navigation instead of memorizing the highway exit number.
theorist: Evan F. Risko & Sam J. Gilbert

name: Google Effect (Digital Amnesia)
definition: The tendency to forget information that can be easily retrieved online, while remembering where and how to access it.
mechanism: Episodic memory consolidation switches from encoding informational content to encoding retrieval paths and search queries.
example: Remembering which folder holds a colleague's research PDF while failing to recall the key percentage in its abstract.
theorist: Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu & Daniel M. Wegner

name: Spatial Memory
definition: The cognitive capability to record, retain, and recall information regarding geographical orientation and spatial configurations.
mechanism: Integrates vestibular, visual, and motor efference signals within the hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex.
example: Remembering where you parked your car in a three-level subterranean parking garage three hours later.

name: Cognitive Dissonance
definition: The distressing mental tension experienced when holding two contradictory beliefs, values, or behaviors simultaneously.
mechanism: Activates the anterior cingulate cortex, prompting rationalization, attitude modification, or belief revision to restore equilibrium.
example: A person who values health continuing to drink sugary sodas by telling themselves 'I exercised yesterday so this one does not count.'

name: Bystander Effect
definition: The social phenomenon wherein individuals are less likely to offer help to a victim when other people are present.
mechanism: Driven by diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance: observers assume someone else has already called for help or that inaction signals safety.
example: Dozens of commuters walking past a person dropped on a busy train platform without stopping because no one else is stopping.

name: Groupthink
definition: A mode of flawed group decision-making where the desire for harmony and consensus overrides realistic critical evaluation of alternatives.
mechanism: Suppresses dissent through self-censorship, perceived unanimity, and stereotyping out-groups under pressure from a charismatic leader.
example: A software team launching a buggy feature on schedule without voicing security doubts because nobody wanted to derail the celebration.

name: Transactive Memory
definition: A shared system for storing and retrieving information where individuals specialize in knowledge domains and rely on partners for recall.
mechanism: Combines individual memory stores with a shared directory of 'who knows what', dramatically multiplying effective cognitive capacity.
example: In a long-term friendship, one person always remembers birthdays and social dates while the other remembers maps and train schedules.

name: Conformity
definition: The act of matching attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors to group norms or peer expectations.
mechanism: Mediated by normative social influence (fear of ostracism) and informational social influence (believing the crowd holds better data).
example: Agreeing that a movie was brilliant in a dinner discussion even though you found it confusing and boring.

name: Obedience to Authority
definition: Compliance with commands given by an perceived authoritative figure, even when the actions conflict with personal conscience.
mechanism: Induces an 'agentic state' where the individual abdicates personal responsibility, viewing themselves merely as an instrument executing orders.
example: An employee shredding financial audit documents simply because a senior executive sternly instructed them to do so immediately.

name: Social Facilitation
definition: The tendency for people to perform simple or well-practiced tasks better in the presence of others than when alone.
mechanism: Mere presence increases physiological autonomic arousal, which enhances dominant responses while impairing complex novel tasks.
example: Running a noticeably faster lap time when jogging beside another runner in the park compared to training solo.

name: Social Loafing
definition: The phenomenon where individuals exert less effort when working collectively in a group than when working individually.
mechanism: Arises from diminished individual accountability and the perception that personal contributions will not be distinctly evaluated.
example: One person barely pushing during a group team tug-of-war match, relying on the combined strength of teammates.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
definition: The cognitive tendency to overestimate personality traits and underestimate situational factors when judging others' actions.
mechanism: Actor perceptual salience: another person's physical body is visually focal, while their external circumstances remain invisible to the observer.
example: Assuming a driver who abruptly swerved past you is an aggressive jerk, without considering they might be rushing to an emergency room.

name: Halo Effect
definition: The cognitive bias where an overall positive impression in one trait (like physical attractiveness) influences judgments in unrelated areas (like intelligence).
mechanism: Memory cognitive efficiency simplifies impressions by forcing all attributes into a congruent evaluative heuristic.
example: Assuming a well-dressed and articulate presenter is also a master software architect without inspecting their underlying code.

name: Confirmation Bias
definition: The tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information that confirms pre-existing beliefs while ignoring contradictions.
mechanism: Protects existing cognitive schemas from dissonance by down-weighting disconfirming evidentiary signals.
example: Only clicking news headlines that align with your political perspective while dismissing contrary investigative reporting as propaganda.

name: Self-Serving Bias
definition: Attributing personal successes to internal dispositions while blaming personal failures on external situational factors.
mechanism: Protects subjective self-esteem and public standing from threats by deflecting negative outcomes outward.
example: Saying 'I worked hard and aced the exam' when scoring well, but saying 'The professor made unfair trick questions' when failing.

name: Stereotype Threat
definition: The situational predicament where people feel at risk of conforming to negative stereotypes about their social group, impairing performance.
mechanism: Triggers acute evaluation anxiety and intrusive self-monitoring, consuming working memory resources needed for the task.
example: Reminding women of math stereotypes immediately before an engineering calculus exam, causing statistically lower scores.

name: Prejudice
definition: A preconceived, typically hostile or unjustified attitude toward members of a group based solely on their group membership.
mechanism: In-group favoritism and out-group derogation driven by social categorization and emotional threat appraisal in the amygdala.
example: Assuming candidates from another university or region lack intellectual rigor before reviewing their work samples.

name: Contact Hypothesis
definition: The theory that interpersonal contact between conflicting groups reduces prejudice under conditions of equal status, shared goals, and institutional support.
mechanism: Humanizes out-group members through individuating information, replacing coarse stereotypes with personal affective connections.
example: Students from rival high schools bonding and overcoming tension while collaborating on a community flood-relief initiative.

name: Reciprocity
definition: A near-universal social norm requiring individuals to return benefits, favors, or kindnesses received from others.
mechanism: Rooted in evolutionary cooperation; unreciprocated favors trigger social guilt and threat of reputational loss.
example: Inviting a neighbor over for dinner because they watered your garden plants while you were traveling.

name: Deindividuation
definition: The loss of individual self-awareness, identity, and personal accountability that occurs in large anonymous crowds or uniform attire.
mechanism: Reduces self-regulation and inner conscience, shifting behavior to mirror immediate situational group impulses.
example: A mild-mannered sports fan shouting insults and knocking over barriers in the stadium because everyone in the mob is doing so.

name: Burnout
definition: A syndrome resulting from chronic unmanaged workplace stress, characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced efficacy.
mechanism: Prolonged HPA axis hyperactivity causes emotional depletion, dopamine receptor downregulation, and cynical detachment.
example: A dedicated nurse feeling emotionally numb, dreading morning shifts, and feeling detached from patients after a year of relentless overtime.

name: Psychological Safety
definition: A shared team belief that the environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, speaking up, and admitting mistakes.
mechanism: Dampens social threat sensitivity in the amygdala, freeing up cognitive bandwidth for candor, curiosity, and rapid error correction.
example: A junior engineer speaking up during an architecture review to point out a potential flaw without fearing humiliation.

name: Two-Factor Theory (Motivator-Hygiene)
definition: Job satisfaction and dissatisfaction arise from independent factors: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, while Motivators drive true engagement.
mechanism: Hygiene satisfies extrinsic safety and physiological baselines; motivators tap intrinsic self-determination and mastery drives.
example: A good salary and ergonomic chair keep an employee from quitting, but challenging projects and autonomy make them love coming to work.

name: Job Crafting
definition: The proactive adjustments employees make to their task boundaries, relationship networks, and cognitive framing of work.
mechanism: Re-establishes personal autonomy and intrinsic value alignment without requiring formal structural organizational changes.
example: A hospital cleaner viewing their daily sanitization work as critical frontline infection prevention that saves patient lives.

name: Expectancy Theory
definition: Motivation is a function of Expectancy (effort leads to performance), Instrumentality (performance leads to reward), and Valence (value of the reward).
mechanism: A cognitive calculation of subjective probabilities; if any single component drops to zero, overall motivation collapses.
example: Working overtime on a proposal only when you genuinely believe the effort will win the client and earn you a meaningful promotion.

name: Equity Theory
definition: Employees evaluate job fairness by comparing their ratio of inputs to outcomes against the perceived ratio of comparable colleagues.
mechanism: Perceived inequity generates distressing cognitive dissonance, motivating individuals to reduce effort, seek raises, or leave.
example: Feeling resentful and pulling back on extra hours after discovering a peer with identical output earns 20% more for less work.

name: Goal-Setting Theory
definition: Specific, challenging goals accompanied by timely feedback lead to substantially higher performance than vague or easy targets.
mechanism: Directs attentional focus, mobilizes sustained effort, fosters persistence, and triggers strategic problem-solving.
example: Aiming to 'reduce API response time by 40% before Friday' produces far greater engineering momentum than 'make the API faster'.

name: Job Demands-Resources Model
definition: Occupational well-being balances high Job Demands (mental strain, deadlines) with Job Resources (autonomy, support, feedback).
mechanism: Excess demands deplete physiological and psychological reserves, while robust resources buffer against burnout and ignite motivation.
example: A software engineer handling tight production deadlines easily because their team provides stellar peer reviews, psychological safety, and flexible hours.

name: Organizational Citizenship Behaviour
definition: Discretionary, voluntary behaviors that are not part of an employee's formal contract, yet promote organizational effectiveness.
mechanism: Driven by affective organizational commitment, reciprocity norms, and intrinsic prosocial motivation.
example: Mentoring a newcomer over lunch or voluntarily tidying up documentation without expecting monetary compensation.

name: Role Conflict
definition: The psychological stress experienced when an individual faces incompatible expectations and demands across different roles or stakeholders.
mechanism: Creates cognitive dissonance and attentional fragmentation as fulfilling one role directly undermines expectations in another.
example: A tech lead caught between management demands to cut testing time and engineering standards to guarantee zero software defects.

name: Emotional Labour
definition: The requirement to manage and display specific emotions (warmth, calmness) as an expected duty of one's professional job role.
mechanism: Surface acting (feigning emotions) creates continuous cognitive dissonance and autonomic strain; deep acting realigns internal feelings.
example: A customer support specialist smiling warmly and speaking pleasantly to an irate client who is yelling over the phone.

name: Self-Determination Theory
definition: A macro-theory of human motivation showing that flourishing depends on satisfying three innate psychological needs: Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness.
mechanism: Transitions extrinsic reward-dependent behaviors into integrated, self-regulated intrinsic motivation.
example: A developer volunteering to build an internal developer tool because they have complete technical freedom and feel valued by colleagues.
theorist: Edward L. Deci & Richard M. Ryan

name: Imposter Phenomenon
definition: The persistent internal belief of being an intellectual fraud despite external evidence of high accomplishment and skill.
mechanism: Attributing achievements to external luck or timing while internalizing minor mistakes as proof of inherent inadequacy.
example: A newly promoted senior engineer fearing every design review is the day their team finally realizes they 'do not know what they are doing.'

name: Transformational Leadership
definition: A leadership approach that inspires followers through charismatic vision, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration to transcend self-interest.
mechanism: Elevates intrinsic motivation and collective identity, aligning individual purpose with a larger societal or technical mission.
example: A research lab director who challenges students to solve unproven problems while offering tailored mentorship and personal encouragement.
theorist: Bernard M. Bass & James MacGregor Burns

name: Job Satisfaction
definition: An evaluative affective and cognitive judgment regarding one's job experience, environment, and occupational rewards.
mechanism: Reflects the gap between personal career expectations and real day-to-day organizational conditions.
example: Feeling energized on Sunday evening because Monday morning brings exciting analytical puzzles and trusted colleagues.

name: Organizational Commitment
definition: The psychological attachment and loyalty an employee feels toward their employing organization (affective, continuance, normative).
mechanism: Synthesizes shared values, perceived exit costs, and moral obligation into an enduring institutional bond.
example: Choosing to stay with a startup through funding turbulence because you believe deeply in its core medical diagnostic vision.

name: Presenteeism
definition: The practice of being physically or virtually present at work while productivity is substantially degraded by illness, stress, or exhaustion.
mechanism: Fear of job insecurity or perceived indispensability forces presence, worsening chronic fatigue and errors.
example: Sitting at your desk staring blankly at code with a pounding fever rather than resting in bed for a day.

name: Bounded Rationality
definition: The concept that human decision-makers cannot be perfectly rational due to cognitive limits, imperfect information, and finite time.
mechanism: Heuristics satisfice rather than optimize, seeking 'good enough' solutions within working-memory processing constraints.
example: Buying the second laptop you inspect in an electronics store because analyzing all 40 models would take all weekend.

name: Loss Aversion
definition: The cognitive reality that the emotional pain of losing something is psychologically about twice as powerful as the pleasure of gaining it.
mechanism: Asymmetrical amygdala and insula activation biases individuals toward risk aversion for gains and risk seeking to avoid losses.
example: Feeling far more devastated over losing a $50 bill than delighted when finding a $50 bill on the sidewalk.

name: Nudge Theory
definition: Designing choice architecture to alter people's behavior in predictable ways without forbidding any options or changing economic incentives.
mechanism: Leverages automatic System 1 heuristics (like default settings) to nudge decisions toward beneficial outcomes.
example: Automatically enrolling new employees into retirement savings plans by default with an option to opt out, boosting savings rates to 90%.

name: Big Five (OCEAN Personality)
definition: A taxonomy of personality across five fundamental dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.
mechanism: Reflects biological neurochemical and behavioral set-points that remain remarkably stable across adulthood.
example: A software architect scoring high in Openness and Conscientiousness enjoying novel deep-tech research while meticulously organizing unit tests.
theorist: Paul Costa & Robert McCrae / Lewis Goldberg

name: Anchoring
definition: The disproportionate influence exerted by the first piece of information encountered on all subsequent estimates and negotiations.
mechanism: Initial numerical values prime semantic memory, anchoring subsequent adjustments insufficiently close to the origin.
example: A car seller first stating $30,000; even after bargaining down to $25,000, you feel you got a great deal though the car is worth $20,000.

name: Framing Effect
definition: Drawing different conclusions from the exact same information depending on whether it is presented as a gain or a loss.
mechanism: Triggers distinct neural risk pathways in the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex depending on semantic valencing.
example: Preferring beef labeled '80% lean' over identical beef labeled '20% fat'.

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
definition: Continuing a failing project or course of action simply because non-recoverable time, money, or effort has already been invested.
mechanism: Desire to avoid admitting loss and waste creates cognitive dissonance, leading to escalating commitment.
example: Finishing a terrible 500-page book you are not enjoying simply because you already read the first 300 pages.

name: Prospect Theory
definition: A behavioral economic model describing how people make decisions between probabilistic alternatives involving risk where outcomes are evaluated relative to a reference point.
mechanism: Replaces expected utility with an S-shaped value function that is concave for gains and convex and steeper for losses.
example: Choosing a guaranteed $500 over a 50% chance at $1,000, but choosing a 50% chance of losing $1,000 over a guaranteed $500 loss.

name: Choice Overload
definition: The paradoxical paralysis and decreased satisfaction that occurs when presented with too many options rather than a curated set.
mechanism: Exhausts working memory and comparison resources, elevating anticipated regret and fear of making a suboptimal choice.
example: Browsing a streaming catalog with 5,000 movies for 45 minutes and ending up watching nothing.

name: Status Quo Bias
definition: An emotional preference for the current state of affairs; baseline conditions are taken as a reference point and changes are viewed as losses.
mechanism: Combines loss aversion with the cognitive effort required to evaluate alternative choices.
example: Staying with an expensive legacy phone plan for six years instead of spending 20 minutes switching to an identical half-price plan.

name: Mere Exposure Effect
definition: The psychological phenomenon whereby people develop a preference for things simply because they are familiar with them.
mechanism: Repeated exposure fosters perceptual fluency; the brain processes familiar stimuli with lower cognitive effort, misattributing fluency as fondness.
example: Disliking a catchy pop song on first listen, but finding yourself humming and enjoying it after hearing it in grocery stores for two weeks.

name: Organizational Culture
definition: The shared values, beliefs, attitudes, and unwritten operational codes that guide how members of an organization interact and work.
mechanism: Transmits tacit behavioral norms via social proof, stories, and reinforcement, establishing collective psychological coherence.
example: A tech team naturally doing blameless postmortems because the engineering group celebrates learning from production crashes.

name: Schein's Culture Model
definition: Culture operates at three depth levels: visible Artifacts, stated Espoused Values, and unconscious Basic Underlying Assumptions.
mechanism: Recognizes that superficial company slogans often disguise deep, invisible survival beliefs that truly drive daily decisions.
example: A company office boasting colorful ping-pong tables (artifact), claiming innovation (value), while secretly firing anyone who fails (underlying assumption).

name: Kotter's Change Model
definition: An eight-step organizational transformation framework starting from establishing urgency up to anchoring new approaches in culture.
mechanism: Addresses status quo inertia and change anxiety by building momentum through early short-term wins and a guiding coalition.
example: A university successfully digitizing its admissions by first demonstrating a pilot system's time savings before mandating it campus-wide.

name: Tuckman's Stages of Group Development
definition: Small groups progress through five predictable social phases: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning.
mechanism: Navigates interpersonal boundaries, status competition, and shared operational scripts to reach high collective competence.
example: A hackathon team moving past early arguments over which framework to use (storming) into seamless synchronized coding sprints (performing).

name: Belbin Team Roles
definition: A taxonomy identifying nine distinct behavioral roles (e.g. Plant, Resource Investigator, Completer Finisher) needed for balanced team synergy.
mechanism: Balances cognitive styles and behavioral tendencies to ensure creativity is checked by practical delivery and cohesion.
example: Pairing a creative visionary who brainstorms wild algorithms with a detail-oriented finisher who spots syntax edge cases.

name: Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions
definition: A cross-cultural framework comparing national cultures across Power Distance, Individualism, Masculinity, Uncertainty Avoidance, and Long-Term Orientation.
mechanism: Maps collective socialization patterns that shape communication protocols and organizational hierarchies across countries.
example: Junior software engineers in high power-distance cultures rarely publicly question a manager's timeline during an all-hands call.

name: Flow
definition: An optimal mental state of complete absorption, focused concentration, and enjoyment in an activity where time seems to stand still.
mechanism: Occurs when task challenge matches personal skill level, inducing transient hypofrontality and silencing self-referential inner chatter.
example: Coding an intricate algorithmic feature for four hours straight and being stunned to discover it is suddenly midnight.

name: PERMA Model of Well-Being
definition: A five-pillar framework of human flourishing: Positive Emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment.
mechanism: Diversifies well-being beyond transient hedonism into durable psychological purpose and social fulfillment.
example: A researcher finding deep satisfaction not just in publishing papers, but in mentoring students and laughing with lab colleagues.

name: Growth Mindset
definition: The belief that abilities, intelligence, and talents can be developed through dedication, strategic effort, and learning from mistakes.
mechanism: Reinterprets failure from an identity threat into informative feedback, sustaining neuroplasticity and persistent effort.
example: Responding to a rejected paper draft by reviewing reviewer critiques enthusiastically to sharpen the mathematical proofs.

name: Learned Optimism
definition: The cultivated habit of explaining setbacks as temporary, specific, and changeable rather than permanent, pervasive, and personal.
mechanism: Alters causal explanatory attributions, dampening feelings of helplessness and energizing constructive agency.
example: Saying 'That specific machine learning model failed because the learning rate was too high' rather than 'I am terrible at data science.'

name: Grit
definition: Passion and sustained perseverance applied toward long-term goals despite adversity, failure, and plateaus in progress.
mechanism: Maintains attentional focus and dopaminergic goal-directed persistence over months and years without immediate external reinforcement.
example: Spending three years debugging, rebuilding, and retesting an assistive vision device until it works reliably in rain and darkness.

name: Gratitude
definition: The conscious emotional recognition and appreciation of positive outcomes, resources, and gifts received from outside oneself.
mechanism: Stimulates the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex, counteracting the evolutionary biological negativity bias.
example: Pausing at night to mentally thank a colleague who took twenty minutes to explain a difficult database query.

name: Broaden-and-Build Theory
definition: Positive emotions broaden an individual's momentary thought-action repertoire, which over time builds enduring physical, intellectual, and social resources.
mechanism: Expands visual and cognitive attentional breadth, fostering creative problem-solving and social bonding.
example: A fun, relaxed brainstorming session sparking a creative machine learning architecture that stressful crunch never could.

name: Hedonic Adaptation (Treadmill)
definition: The observed tendency of humans to quickly return to a stable baseline level of happiness despite major positive or negative events.
mechanism: Habituation dampens neurochemical response to repeated sensory or emotional rewards to maintain sensitivity to new environmental signals.
example: Feeling thrilled for two weeks after buying the latest smartphone, only for it to feel ordinary and unremarkable by month two.

name: Resilience
definition: The capacity to recover quickly from difficulties, adapt flexibly to trauma or adversity, and sustain psychological equilibrium.
mechanism: Supported by prefrontal regulation of the amygdala, a strong social support network, and an internal locus of control.
example: Dusting off after losing a major funding pitch, analyzing the judges' feedback, and submitting a refined proposal two days later.

name: Self-Efficacy
definition: An individual's belief in their capability to execute the behaviors necessary to achieve specific performance attainments.
mechanism: Built through mastery experiences, vicarious modeling, social persuasion, and management of somatic anxiety states.
example: Tackling an unfamiliar deep learning library with confidence because you have already mastered three complex frameworks in the past.

name: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction
definition: An evidence-based program that combines secular mindfulness meditation and gentle movement to cultivate non-judgmental present-moment awareness.
mechanism: Reduces grey-matter volume in the amygdala while strengthening functional connectivity between the prefrontal cortex and insula.
example: Noticing a surge of anger during a tense email exchange, taking three slow conscious breaths, and letting the sensation pass without lashing out.

name: Character Strengths (VIA Classification)
definition: A universal taxonomy of 24 positive human traits organized under six core virtues: Wisdom, Courage, Humanity, Justice, Temperance, and Transcendence.
mechanism: Deploying signature strengths generates authentic energy and intrinsic fulfillment compared to fixing minor deficiencies.
example: Using your signature strength of 'Love of Learning' to read foundational computer science papers on weekends with joy.

name: Savouring
definition: The conscious attention to, appreciation of, and deliberate prolongation of positive experiences and pleasurable feelings.
mechanism: Interrupts habituation and sensory adaptation by holding the positive stimulus in working memory for deeper affective encoding.
example: Slowly sipping your morning coffee while feeling the sunlight on your face instead of checking phone notifications.

name: Post-Traumatic Growth
definition: Positive psychological change experienced as a result of the struggle with highly challenging, traumatic life crises.
mechanism: Requires deep cognitive restructuring of one's fundamental life schemas, yielding greater personal strength, closer relationships, and revised priorities.
example: Recovering from a life-threatening illness with a renewed sense of purpose to dedicate your engineering skills to medical diagnostics.

name: Hope Theory
definition: A motivational model defining hope as the perceived capability to derive pathways to desired goals, along with the agency to use them.
mechanism: Combines Pathways Thinking (generating workable alternative routes) with Agency Thinking (sustaining motivation along the path).
example: When a cloud server provider crashes right before a project presentation, calmly deploying a pre-tested local fallback container.

name: Self-Compassion
definition: Treating oneself with kindness, recognition of shared humanity, and mindful awareness when facing personal pain or perceived inadequacy.
mechanism: Downregulates the threat defense system (self-criticism) and activates the mammalian caregiving attachment system (oxytocin).
example: Comforting yourself after failing a job interview like you would comfort a dear friend, rather than engaging in harsh internal insults.

name: Emotional Intelligence (EQ)
definition: The ability to monitor, discriminate, and understand one's own and others' emotions, and use this information to guide thought and action.
mechanism: Integrates fronto-limbic circuitry, allowing emotional signals to inform reasoning without hijacking executive control.
example: Recognizing that your irritability in an afternoon meeting is simply low blood sugar, choosing to pause for a snack before responding.
theorist: Peter Salovey & John Mayer / Daniel Goleman

name: Operant Conditioning
definition: A learning process in which the strength and probability of a voluntary behavior is modified through reinforcement or punishment.
mechanism: Dopaminergic reward prediction pathways in the basal ganglia reinforce synaptic connections between situational cues and rewarded actions.
example: Studying extra hours after receiving praise and a high grade on a research paper.

name: Classical Conditioning
definition: A learning procedure in which a biologically potent unconditioned stimulus is paired with a previously neutral stimulus to elicit a learned response.
mechanism: Forms associative synaptic linkages in the lateral amygdala or cerebellum so that the neutral cue triggers reflexive autonomic arousal.
example: Feeling your heart rate spike upon hearing a specific alarm chime that previously accompanied middle-of-the-night emergency server outages.

name: Shaping (Successive Approximations)
definition: A behavioral method of teaching a complex target behavior by reinforcing successive approximations of the desired action.
mechanism: Gradually narrows the reinforcement window, incrementally conditioning neural motor programs toward the target mastery state.
example: Teaching a child to swim by first rewarding splashing feet in shallow water, then putting their face in, then floating with support.

name: Latent Learning
definition: Learning that occurs without explicit immediate reinforcement or obvious behavioral changes, becoming apparent only when an incentive is introduced.
mechanism: Forms internal cognitive maps and schemas through passive environmental exploration, stored implicitly until task motivation activates recall.
example: Driving a coworker home without ever having driven there yourself, simply because you rode along as a passenger on three previous occasions.

name: Habit Formation (The Habit Loop)
definition: The process by which a behavior becomes automatic through repeated execution in response to a specific contextual Cue, Routine, and Reward.
mechanism: Shifts behavioral control from the conscious prefrontal cortex to automatic chunked circuitry in the dorsolateral striatum.
example: Sitting down at your desk with your morning tea (cue), opening your task checklist immediately (routine), and feeling organized (reward).

name: Reinforcement Schedules
definition: Rules determining whether a behavior is reinforced continuously or intermittently based on fixed or variable ratios and intervals.
mechanism: Variable ratio schedules induce maximal behavioral resistance to extinction by producing continuous dopaminergic anticipation.
example: Checking a social feed or slot machine repeatedly because unpredictable variable rewards keep curiosity at peak intensity.

name: Extinction
definition: The gradual weakening and eventual disappearance of a conditioned response when the behavior is no longer reinforced or paired with the unconditioned stimulus.
mechanism: Does not erase the original memory; instead, the infralimbic cortex forms a new inhibitory memory trace that suppresses expression.
example: A dog eventually stopping begging at the dinner table after family members strictly refuse to feed it any scraps for a month.

name: Observational Learning (Social Learning)
definition: Learning that occurs through observing, retaining, and replicating the behaviors and outcomes demonstrated by social models.
mechanism: Engages frontoparietal mirror neuron systems to simulate actions and predict consequences without experiencing direct personal trials.
example: A student mastering Git branch rebasing by watching their mentor's terminal screen during a live pair-programming session.

name: Learned Helplessness
definition: A condition in which a person or animal learns that they have no control over painful stimuli, and consequently gives up trying even when escape is possible.
mechanism: Uncontrollable stressors hyperactivate dorsal raphe serotonin circuits, turning off active escape motivation in the striatum.
example: A student failing two math quizzes and concluding 'I simply lack a math brain', completely stopping all study efforts even with a private tutor.

name: Negative Reinforcement
definition: Increasing the frequency of a behavior by removing or avoiding an unpleasant or aversive stimulus when the behavior occurs.
mechanism: Relief from distress produces a negative reward prediction error, strengthening the neural pathways that enacted the escape.
example: Fastening your car seatbelt immediately to silence the irritating and persistent warning chime.

name: Punishment (Positive & Negative)
definition: A behavioral consequence that decreases the likelihood of a target behavior recurring (either by introducing an aversive event or removing a valued one).
mechanism: Activates threat and avoidance circuits in the insula and amygdala, suppressing immediate behavioral expression.
example: Receiving a speeding ticket fine (positive punishment) or losing driving privileges for a month (negative punishment).

name: Stimulus Generalization
definition: The tendency for a conditioned response to be evoked by stimuli that are similar to the original conditioned stimulus.
mechanism: Reflects overlapping receptive fields in sensory cortices before fine-grained discriminative tuning has taken place.
example: A child bitten by a small terrier subsequently feeling afraid of all breeds of dogs, whether big or small.

name: Stimulus Discrimination
definition: The learned ability to differentiate between similar stimuli and respond only to the specific stimulus paired with reinforcement.
mechanism: Cortical sharpening enhances contrast between neural activation patterns, preventing non-reinforced cues from triggering responses.
example: Recognizing the subtle ringtone of your own phone in a crowded room while ignoring ten other ringing phones.

name: Spontaneous Recovery
definition: The reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest period without any further conditioning trials.
mechanism: Proves that extinction is active inhibition rather than unlearning; the inhibitory trace decays slightly faster over time than the conditioned memory.
example: Suddenly craving a cigarette or feeling nostalgia upon visiting your old college town years after quitting smoking.

name: Token Economy
definition: A systematic contingency management system where targeted desirable behaviors are reinforced with secondary tokens that can be exchanged for backup rewards.
mechanism: Bridges the temporal gap between immediate action and distant gratification by providing concrete intermediate markers of progress.
example: A classroom rewarding students with stickers for completing homework, which can be traded on Friday for 15 minutes of free drawing time.

name: Premack Principle (Grandma's Rule)
definition: A higher-probability, naturally favored behavior can be used as an effective reinforcer for a lower-probability, less preferred behavior.
mechanism: Leverages the brain's existing motivational drive for pleasurable tasks to overcome resistance to effortful or tedious duties.
example: Permitting yourself to play video games for an hour only after completing two practice problem sets in discrete mathematics.

name: Behavioural Activation
definition: A structured therapeutic approach that encourages individuals to systematically schedule and engage in positive, rewarding activities to counter depression.
mechanism: Breaks the depressive cycle of avoidance and inactivity by re-establishing environmental contact with positive dopaminergic reinforcement.
example: Scheduling a 20-minute morning walk and a phone call with a friend when feeling unmotivated, sparking renewed daily energy.

name: Law of Effect
definition: Responses that produce a satisfying effect in a particular situation become more likely to occur again, while discomforting responses become less likely.
mechanism: The historical foundational principle of behavioral learning: biological consequences directly sculpt subsequent behavioral repertoire.
example: A cat learning to press an escape lever in a puzzle box faster and faster with each successive trial to reach food.
